p: If nothing– oh, go ahead.
If creating fear and creating the discomfort and fear to the ridership, we have in the past charged that aggravated harassment statute as discussed by the Commissioner.
And just one more. A kosher restaurant being vandalized with “Kill the Zionists.” Is that hate crime?

So, it’s going to depend. This is the work of the Hate Crimes Taskforce to investigate, right? Like, this is exactly what they have to do, right, to be able to prove that it was because of the person’s, you know, Jewish identity in whole or in substantial part. I

mean, it wasn’t a pure, you know, call it political motivation. It could be both, obviously. It could be both. You could imagine it being in part political and in part anti-Jewish, right? We have to be able to prove that. That’s the work of the taskforce to be able to prove that. If we can prove it, we’ll charge it.
And if it just says “Kill the Jews,” do you see that as different?
If– I’m sorry, if?
Says “Kill the Jews.”
No, that’s a hate crime right there. That’s– that is clearly because of a perceived Jewishness or Jewish identity and that would be charged as a hate crime. That would be charged as a hate crime.

Okay. On December 15th, 2025, the second night of Hanukkah, 20-year-old Minocum Risemen [sp?], an Orthodox Habad member, was attacked on the Three Train towards Crown Heights. The attacker shouted “F the Jews” on the video at the outset of the assault. The Department’s initial

classification was argument over seats, not a hate crime. It was only after community outcry that the hate crime classification was restored. Can you walk us through who made that initial classification, what the Hate Crime Taskforce reviewed before making it and what role the hate crime review panel played in this?

Council Member, I am not familiar with the particulars of that case. I could not tell you sitting here kind of what went into that, who was making what decisions, what the analysis was. I just don’t know.
That’s fine. If you could look into it and get back to us.
Sure.
We would appreciate it. And I want to talk to you a little bit about the incident that took place in my district two nights ago. I think you saw the video.
I’ve seen the video, yes.

So, you know what occurred. There was a protest at a location where the individuals often protest. They usually don’t

march after they protest. This time, they decided to march onto a street with a synagogue and a daycare, intimidating students. There was a Rabbi inside, and I talked about this in my opening statement. There’s a Rabbi inside training a boy for a bar mitzvah. Parents called me infuriated, intimidated, and feared for the safety of their children. So, and just to be fair, they did not according to the videos I’ve seen, they did not block any entrances. So, I just have a couple of questions as it regards to this incident and more broadly. Do officers receive training on handling these protests?

Right. So, we have– as part of the protest settlement. There’s actually all sorts of training that goes on. Community Affairs gets training. Our executives get training. We’ve separately been talking with executives in particular about how to handle situations involving protests outside houses of worship or outside of schools or other sensitive locations. So, yeah, there’s the formal piece as far as the protest settlement, but there’s also work that we’ve been doing really at the executive level, captains and above, to make sure they understand how

this works. At least say COs and above and how this works in terms of handling protests outside, like I said, shuls, schools, other sensitive locations.

And is sensitivity training a part of that? Just because, as you may know, it’s important for officers that are going to protests to understand the sensitivities, especially again that’s next to a synagogue or a Jewish daycare, to understand why mass protestors shouting hateful slogans. It’s very traumatizing to the Jewish community.

Yeah, and I do think– I’m not sure I can speak to like sensitivity training across the Department. There’s all sorts of training that goes on, just you’re not talk– these are not– we’re not the right people to I think really speak to that, but I do think that for example their COs their job is to know their communities. Community Affairs officers, they do– they do understand this. I don’t think the point your making about the sensitives here, I don’t think that's lost on the CO of that command, the Community Affairs officers involved, leadership of the Department. We definitely understand that.

Okay. And is there an NYPD directive as to conduct when a sudden protest emerges and ends up directly outside of a house worship or a day care facility. But when they’re not– specifically when they’re not blocking the entrance. So, yesterday I had a call with the NPYP, and they cited free speech, and I’m very supportive of the First Amendment and I totally believe in free speech, but I know there are also limits and I know we have– we can put in time, place and manner restrictions. So, I’m wondering in the case of what happened two nights ago, what could have been done differently, legally within the authority of the NYPD. And I know there’s a consent decree and I know there’s a consent decree and I know that you're somewhat limited. But what could have been done differently to prevent protestors intimidating parents and children and worshipers?

Right. So, as you know, this was in some ways an unusual situation. What I mean is, this was a group that had protested before at a different location, a commercial location and had been stationary in prior instances. Right? So we really had no set– and

those I think have gone without incident, and again, stationary in a small, relatively small group, small group, small counter group. And so we did not know in advance. I had no reason to think in advance that they would be marching. And so that was a surprise. It was. We don’t have a crystal ball. And we did not have a lot of resources there. We didn’t. So, in that situation– so they start marching, limited resources. I think given what– if they had– let’s just say. So if they had come to that schools– and they were marching across various blocks, right? I think they– this was one of many blocks they marched down the other day. If they had, for example stopped– like a few scenarios. One, if they had stoped and obstructed entrance, we would have, you know, given them a warning and if they failed to move, they’d be subject to arrest. If they had stopped at that location and were going to set up there let’s say to protest there for any meaningful period of time, we would have been concerned about obstruction, right? And we would have– we would have gotten– we would have set up a frozen zone in front of the entrance there to make sure there was no obstructing, people getting in and out without

incident. We would have worked to move them across the street. You have to make sure they have sight and sound. They were going to set up there. But make sure we have that frozen zone there with barriers as necessary. Given the video that I saw, they actually were moving along. They actually did not stop there. They were continuing down that street as they had on other occasions, as they had on other streets. And so in that scenario, there’s nothing– I’m not sure there’s really anything for the PD to do in that moment because they’re moving along. They’re going. I do agree that given that we know and that we’ve experienced, this is a group that actually– if they gather again to protest that same commercial location, they may march. We got to think in advance about where they’re going to march, plan for that, and part of that is trying to talk to the organizers. Sometimes they’ll talk to us, sometimes they won’t. It’s thinking about how we can enable them to march, and as you said, you know, exercise that first amendment right. It doesn’t mean they can march wherever they want whenever they want, right? And we have to sort of plan it out in advance, and part of that is having resources in the right place. They

were on the sidewalk. They are times when we say the folks who are mentioned, listen, you can go here or you can go here, or you know, you can straight or you can go right, but you’re not going to be able take this left turn. If it’s the sidewalk, though it means we’re closing the street. In other words, if a sidewalk is otherwise open to the public, we can’t say it’s open to the public except for the protestors. That we can’t do. That’s a problem. That would be content-based speech regulation, and that we can’t do. So, given what transpired, going forward, would we planned for this protest very differently? Yes, 100 percent. How exactly we’re going to structure it? We got to figure that out. I do want to emphasize though, again, just for the cops who were there in the moment, they were surprised. I think they were doing their best in the situation. It would be very, very different if the protestors had stopped and looked like they were going to remain there for a meaningful period of time. We would have had to really sort of address potential obstruction risks. Given the video that I saw, that’s not what happened.

I’m assuming this is not the first surprise you’ve had with protests where they marched afterwards to a location. So, that’s why I’m wondering if there’s a specific directive that NYPD has to the COs or to the entire NYPD regarding what conduct officers need to engage in if protestors are walking and shouting right by houses of worship and educational facilities, or is there no directive and it’s just case by case basis?

Well, there is– no, there are very clear directives in terms of concerns about obstruction, about sight and sound. If people are set up, right? So, again, if they had said– if the protestors had come and said, okay, we’re going to be protesting outside this Jewish elementary school, we would have a lot– there’s a lot we have to say about how that works consistent with the law, consistent with the First Amendment, but also consistent with the safety and security of people inside, and we would set up for that, right? And they would not be right there in front of the entrance, probably across the street. Again, sight and sound– we have appropriate barrier configuration,

police officers there if necessary. We would do all that, and that’s very clear.
There is a directive?
What I’ve just described is, I think, very clear to the leadership in the Department. Again–
[interposing] Do you have that in writing? Can we get a copy of that?

We have– no, this is a– this is directive that maybe I have given and descriptions I have given to the leadership of the Department, to executives in the Department. We have gone over this. I think they know it very well. I just want to emphasize again that what you have here, we [inaudible] day, and again, I understand– I truly do understand why this was upsetting to the people who were inside. I am not minimizing that in any way. It is the case, though, that they did not remain there and they– I can tell from the video were moving right along. They were, and that does change the analysis.
So, could we have moved them across the street?
But they were already moving down the block. It was no– I mean, again, they weren’t stationary. They were moving down the block already.

But before they moved to the synagogue and the daycare center, could we have just directed them? Could the NYPD have just directed them to move across the street, go around the synagogue and the daycare center and come back to the sidewalk?

So, if we were– if we knew, if we had known in advance they were going to go there and we were concerned about obstruction, we could do a frozen zone around the entrance to the school. We could close off part of the block, however you want to do it, but you have to consider the counter-protestors who were across the street. Like the goal is not to tell the protestors to go stand where the counter-protestors are standing. That’s a recipe for problems. And yeah, we could 100 percent– if we had– if we had known in advance that they were going to go there, we could have certainly have done a frozen there and avoided a

situation if they were right there moving past the entrance. Again, we didn’t know that was going to happen, and we did not have the barriers there in advance. We didn’t have the resources there in advance. Now that we know this is a possibility, we’re going to plan accordingly.

Okay. Thank you. I just have a couple of more questions. Just want refer you to the penal law 2421 and I’ll just read it in part. A person is guilty of disruption or disturbance of a religious service when he or she makes unreasonable noise or disturbance while at a lawfully-assembled religious service or within 300 feet thereof with intent to cause annoyance or alarm or recklessly creating a risk thereof. Disruption or disturbance of a religious service is a Class A misdemeanor. So, based on the fact that we just discussed, I assume that what we saw in the video is an accurate description of what happened, may this behavior be considered a Class A misdemeanor under Section 24021 of the New York City Penal Law?

No, I really don’t think so. I don’t. I mean, again, [inaudible] all the information. I did see the video. These

were individuals– these individuals were walking down which was a publicly accessible sidewalk. They were legally allowed to be there, were not obstructing anything. I don’t have any evidence of their intent to disrupt what was going on inside. I don’t, and again, I’m not– that is consistent with– I want to acknowledge this again, kind of the pain and the frustration, I get it, of people who are in there or learned about in the community. Not minimizing that. But do I think that those individuals walking past there in the way that they were under these circumstances were committing a crime? I don’t think they were committing a crime.

They were making– we could say they were making unreasonable noise. We could argue that. They were within 300 feet of the synagogue and the daycare center. They were likely doing it with the intent to cause annoyance or alarm, recklessly creating a risk thereof, and that type of disruption according to Penal Law 24021 is a Class A misdemeanor.

I got to say, though, at least on what I have, information that I have, I don’t have the evidence of

unreasonable noise, and I don’t have the evidence of intent. I think it matters a lot. They were walking along– I mean, it’s multiple blocks, right? It was one of the many blocks they walked down. We don’t have the evidence that they were targeting this location. We don’t have the evidence of unreasonable noise. I just– on the facts as I understand them that I’m aware of, I do not think you have a crime there.
You don’t have the evidence because it happened two nights ago, and I don’t think we had the time to investigate.

Again, I have the information that I have. I really do not see evidence of a crime here. And I want to emphasize again that when you have publicly accessible street, there’s no frozen zone. They’re allowed to be there. They’re allowed to march there. To the extent you’re suggesting that the fact they were marching there with the message that they had, that in and of itself would give rise to a criminal charge, I do not think that is correct, again, with the facts that I have.
Even without investigating the incident?

I’m not sure– I mean, again, if someone wants ot make a complaint, they can make a complaint. Anyone is free to make a complaint, and we will take that complaint. We will investigate it accordingly. But I just want to emphasize– but I just have to acknowledge, right, public street not closed off, that’s– people are allowed to march down that street. That’s what the First Amendment is.

Okay. thank you for that explanation. And just so I know what to tell my constituents that are very concerned, what can be done in the future other than setting up buffer zones in case of obstruction of entrances, but what I can tell them to make them feel that their children are going to be safe? And I’m not just talking about this particular incident, but I’m sure we’re going to see a lot of protests and marches that walk by and intimidate worshippers and daycare centers.

Right. I think there are a few things to be said. First of all, there is an open line of communication to the NYPD directly. We are happy to engage with

individuals from the school, with Community Affairs or otherwise, the leadership of the school so we can hear directly from them. I think that is totally appropriate, and if they want to do that, we are more than open to that. They should know that the NYPD takes this responsibility for public safety extremely seriously. We do this every day. Yes, we have– there’s a real challenge, right? We have to both make sure we’re ensuring First Amendment rights and ensuring that people are safe. We do this to the very best of our ability, and I think they– we are going to take a hard look at certainly in this area, right, in terms of if protestors are marching going forward, how are we going to handle that. Again, consistent with the First Amendment, allowing people to march, and if we have to do more in terms of frozen zones, then we’ll do what we have to do to make sure that this is all safe.
Okay. Thank you. Those are all my questions, and I appreciate the open line of communication. And thank you for the service of the NYPD. Thank you.

Listening to some of the answers of the questions, it’s very

interesting to hear, but there are directives for what the protocol is around protesting around schools and houses of worship, and it’s my opinion and the opinion of this council, actually, that those directives should be transparent and there should be time for public input. And when you say schools and protestors can always reach out to you, that it should be very clear on a public plan who the point person is at the NYPD. That is in fact a law that we passed in this council, one that will provide much needed transparency to avoid incidents like this altogether. So, community members, protestors, schools, houses of worship, everyone under the sun knows what they’re getting and knows who to contact, and that there is community input for that. That is what we passed in this council and I look forward to it becoming law so we can increase the amount of transparency in our NYPD. I was– one of the questions Council Member– Chair Vernikov asked was, there’s a kosher restaurant and someone spray paints, vandalizes and writes zionist on it. And you said maybe it’s a hate crime. And then if you use the word Jew it’s definitely a hate crime. I– we’ve just seen time and time again where the word zionist is

used as a proxy, and– for Jew, right? Where we’ve seen in our city kosher restaurants who never made a political statement in their life vandalized and spray painted zionist and a Jewish star on it. Like, there should be no question that those would be hate crimes, and I think what you’ve delivered is sort of like the out saying the NYPD does not necessarily– if you just use the word zionist instead of Jew, then it– then you might be okay.

We have to follow the law. We have to follow the law, and the law does distinguish between– so, a few things. One, it distinguishes between crimes because of one’s religious identity and one because of– it’s called a political view point. I understand what you are saying, and I’m not naïve about this. Of course, it may very well be the case, very well be the case, the person when they vandalized that store and they say zionist that that is an anti-Jewish hate crime. That is not lost on me. We have to be able to prove that. I’d have to be able to prove it. That’s– we have to be able to prove it. And so that’s the work of the hate crimes taskforce, and if we can prove that, we will charge it. We are not shy about doing that.

We also have to follow the law, and the law says we have to be able to prove that it’s because of religious identity. So, that’s what we do. We are applying the law to the very best ability and investigating these cases very aggressively and very deliberately and very carefully so that we can charge hate crimes when we have the evidence.

I want to– Executive Director Wisdom, you had mentioned earlier in your testimony that you will model the report after the Biden administration, right? In their report, they laid out examples of when the anti-zionism crosses into anti-semitism. They tried to make it explicit and clear. They used the nexus document and the [inaudible] definition to make clear, like these are the examples of how the Jewish community is experiencing antisemitism. Do you expect that to be part of your work? Laying out the examples so that the city knows that when you do spray paint zionist as a slur, which is not, on a kosher restaurant simply because it’s kosher, that that is in fact– from an educational standpoint, not from prosecutorial standpoint, from an educational

standpoint, are you including– do you plan to include any of those examples or that work in your report?

Thank you for the question, Chair Dinowitz. I want to clarify that we’re modeling the process after the Biden Whitehouse process. And so that’s just about who we’re talking to, how we’re talking to them, providing a framework. In terms of the actual layout of the document, I am not yet sure, but I do imagine that we will be getting into some of these secure [sic] questions, and at least publishing a statement of sort of principles and values about what antisemitism is without using a specific definition.

Yeah, well, we’ve– well, as you know, the Biden administration didn’t use a specific definition. They modeled it on those two definitions which are good definitions. Obviously, the vast majority of the Jewish community values those two definitions. And at schools like NYU, which a university here in New York City that did lay out of examples where anti-zionism is very clearly antisemitism. They have seen a decrease in antisemitic incidents, right? And so that’s what I’m asking of you. If you’re not addressing this issue

in your report, because this is what people are reporting that zionist is a proxy for Jew, right? And this is very often where they get turned away from– by the patrol officers which we’ve spoken about. I don’t want to rehash that.

No, I do want to be clear, though, if I may. Of course, the Hate Crimes Taskforce would investigate that, and again, if we have the evidence, we will charge it as a hate crime, anti-Jewish hate crime, but we need to have the evidence. We have to.

I agree that we need to be contending with what are sort of the stickier examples of what constitute antisemitism, and again, I don’t know yet what form that will take, but understand that this is the crux of this conversation, and is one that we will certainly be addressing in one form or another.
Yeah. I mean, you now even have people saying “zio.” They’re throwing “zio” as like a slur.
I believe David Duke invented that slur.

That’s correct. That is correct. But you have people on all sides of the aisle using this white supremacist invented term as a slur against Jewish people. So, I would impress upon you how important it is that this sort of language is outlined, and when we have seen it outlined and seen it– you know, it identified as that, it gives people the confidence still that if they report it– it gives people the tools to know if they report it to the NYPD it won’t go unnoticed. It’ll give them the confidence to go to the NYPD and report actual hate crimes, because again, there is significant under-reporting, and it’s under-reporting because at times NYPD doesn’t take it seriously or at times they just don’t feel that the city and the city agencies understand. Your work, the work you do individually and together is critical in identifying and reporting. And I lastly want to ask about bias incidents. So, Chair Vernikov went through a few examples, and you highlighted that sometimes it’s free speech, and sometimes it’s a hate crime, but regardless calling someone an f-ing Jew is an act of bias, right? That’s a bias incident.
Yes.
I don’t– it’s not clear to me how the NYPD defines bias versus hate crime, but the important thing is for my question, it’s a bias incident. No matter what the law says–
[interposing] Yes.
it is felt as a bias incident. What happens to those bias incidents? To where do they get reported and where is that data?

So, a few things are going to happen, right? So, the Community Affairs is going to be notified, notifications up the chain, and there’ll be a notification to the Hate Crimes Taskforce which will look at the incident, because there are two pieces to this, right? One, let’s assume the facts are just that. Right? It’s just a slur, nothing else.
So, a slur walking down the street, they report it, right?

Nothing else, yeah. So, it’s not a crime without more, but there still may be a need for outreach, right? Community Affairs following up with that individual, with the local school, the local shul, maybe. The

Community Affairs piece, because obviously that individual is going to be upset. The community is going to be upset. People may be concerned. So there’s an outreach piece. Separately, there’s– the Hate Crimes Taskforce opening a case to make sure we have the full picture of what happened.
Does the Hate Crimes Taskforce really opening a case when it’s a slur?

Well, they’re going to go talk to the complainant to make sure there wasn’t anything else going on. So, because– and to your point, right, this is about making it– trying to make it as easy as possible for complainants and engaging with complainants. You can imagine a situation in which initially you only hear about the slur, and then there’s follow-up from trained detectives and you learn more. This person was following me for several blocks. This person was– this person pushed me. I was actually trying to cross the street and this person blocked me from crossing the street. Any number of things. You can easily imagine this happening, right? They focus on the slur because it’s so jarring and hurtful and

hateful. There are other things that have legal significance that the detectives elicit, and– all of a sudden, actually, now you have a hate crime, right? Because if there’s conduct that’s married up with that, we’re going to, you know, go make an arrest and charge a hate crime, if you see what I mean. So that’s why it actually is really important for Hate Crimes Taskforce to get these when they first come in so they can have a full picture of the facts.

Yeah, so there’s two separate things I will say it again. I think it’s work an audit of your– of the NYPD worth retraining, because there are officers out there, if it’s more than zero it’s too many, who will hear this story, say, you know, someone called me the whatever word, and they’ll say there’s no really crime committed, sorry. And then they’ll turn them away. And of course, that discourages people from reporting anything at all. But in addition to that, the ones that aren’t– that don’t include the harassment, the ones that don’t include blocking and obstruction, the ones that don’t include following them, is that data collected and is it reported, and is it– and importantly, is it shared with the Mayor’s Office to

Combat Antisemitism which would then address, alright, it’s not a hate crime, but it– there is hate going on in the community, and their job is to address hate. So, is that data collected?

Right. So that data of everything coming into the Hate Crimes Taskforce is what we’re now reporting on for the first time, right? That’s going to be in that universe of possible of reported hate crimes, even though it’s not going to pan– it may or may not pan out. If the facts are just a slur, nothing more, it’s not going to pan out. It will not be confirmed as a hate crime, but it will be included in that universe of cases that the Hate Crimes Taskforce opened. And then in terms of the data sharing, we do share with the– go ahead.

So, in cases of violent hate crimes, crimes against persons, for instance, that is shared within 72 hours to OPHC for their outreach and work that they do. The metric is now going to be reported out as the Commissioner explained, but there is communication between Hate Crime Taskforce and OPHC in those cases of crimes against persons that rise.

Alright. We as Council Members get outreach when a violent hate crime occurs. We don’t get notification when a hate crime occurs which should change, and I have a bill on that, by the way. So, I’ll sign on. I’m going to move on to another round for Council Member Felder, followed by Council Member Brewer and Council Member Epstein.

Thank you. Okay, thank you. I admire your persistence. No, no, I mean it in– I mean it very much, because it’s a very complicated issue. I just– it’s just in my mind it’s so hard to get a permit even to put up, you know, some rides for the holiday that it just seems odd. So, thank you for trying. I want to– you know, I want to go back to the question that Chair Vernikov and I should say– talked about the distinctions between zionist and Jew, and I– it’s not to you. It’s to my favorite person at the desk, because I know that she feels very, very left out of, you know– I just want to– it’s not a question. So, I just want to tell you that everything that I’ve read– I’m not a lawyer in any way, and I don’t read much. In fact, I hire staff to read everything and give me bullet points

which was– if it would be– I’d be in school for 50 [sic] years, got an ADHD, I would be like the king. So, I just want to tell you that everything that I've read indicates that the Mayor does not consider calling somebody a zionist in any way hate speech or the– I should– let me correct that. Erase. The equivalent of calling somebody a Jew. That calling somebody a zionist and calling somebody a Jew are by no means in any way the same in any way. If you want, I can get you some more material that indicates that publicly. Second, when I asked you whether you experienced antisemitism, the example you gave me indicates that you never experienced antisemitism personally. You felt it. You felt it. I’m not going to indicate about somebody’s feelings in any way. I just will tell you what to me is experiencing antisemitism. It is a four-year-old names Simcha Felder walking down the street and somebody knocking him to the ground and calling him an f-ing Jew. I didn’t feel that. That was that. Or waking up one morning, coming outside as a 10-year-old and finding a swastika that was spray painted on our house. So, again, it’s not a competition. I just really, really am bothered by the fact that you seem like a very

nice person and I’m not judging your character or how much hate you’ve encountered if– you know, maybe there are other experiences, and I’m not suggesting that you shouldn’t have been bothered by what you saw, but when we talk about antisemitism and hate in this city, I would just hope that you in addition to running this area that you have people on your staff that have actually personally– and personally really experienced hate and antisemitism physically and emotionally. And it just– you know, I would hope so. That’s all. So, I want to thank the Chairs for the hearing and there are so many people here that have been waiting to testify and unfortunately again we have other hearings that are again conflict with the ones we have and people are going to have to leave. So, I’m going to give you back the 47 seconds that I took last time.
Would you want to respond, Ms. Wisdom?

Yeah, I guess, I mean, I completely appreciate what you’re saying. I hope that someday you and I will have a chance to sit down and get to know each other, and I’ll have more than 30 seconds to talk about my

experiences with antisemitism beyond what’s happened in the last 24 hours. But I take very seriously the safety of every single Jewish person in this city, across religiosity, identity, race, and understand very acutely the differences between how we experience antisemitism. But if my answer indicated to you that what I saw yesterday is the only experience I’ve had with antisemitism, I will clarify on the record that that’s not the case.

Thank you. And I have some questions for the Mayor’s office. Ms. Wisdom, I think it’s no secret that– and I speak on behalf of my community when I say that we are deeply dissatisfied with the way this mayor has handled antisemitism. That being said, I heard really great things about you personally and your character and your competence, and I do want to work with you and look forward to talking. I know we didn’t have a chance to sit down. But I think that there’s been virtually no information about this office that the public has been given. They don’t know what this office is about, who’s in charge. So we do have some questions for you. Can you talk a little bit about what– I’ll skip because I know you’re pressed for

time. Just tell us as Executive Director can you tell us what your job is at this office?

sure. I’m the Executive Director of the Mayor's Office to Combat Antisemitism. It’s an office that’s just under a year old. We’re building a staff right now.
